sections.html:
Tupelo is the seat of Lee County in northeast Mississippi, roughly halfway between Memphis and Birmingham. The 2020 census counted 37,923 residents, the seventh highest total in the state, and the city serves as a commercial and industrial hub for the region. It covers about 51 square miles along Interstate 22 and U.S. Route 78.

There were 17,102 housing units in 2020, 9.5 percent of them vacant. Owner-held homes were rarely empty, with a homeowner vacancy rate of 1.5 percent, while the rental vacancy rate was 13.3 percent. Most sellers deal with two governments: the City of Tupelo for permits and code, and Lee County for property tax.

Tupelo has a documented tornado history, so a patched roof or a repaired wall is likely to draw questions in an inspection. A seller with repair paperwork ready can answer them quickly.

The Department of Development Services handles permits, building, planning and code enforcement, and it will not approve a permit without a current recorded deed. It is on the third floor of City Hall at 71 East Troy Street. Permitting staff can be reached at 662-841-6510 or permits@tupeloms.gov.

Code Enforcement helps owners comply with the city's ordinances and Development Code, and owners are responsible for keeping property in compliance. A letter of violation or citation has to be resolved with that office, and fines can follow if it is not. The city publishes a rental inspection checklist and property maintenance standards, and the Building Division runs a Blight and Demolition Program.

  • Check for open violations before you list, since they can surface in a buyer's due diligence.
  • If you rent the house, ask Permitting about the rental inspection process.
  • Gather permits for past work, because every application needs a recorded deed.

Parts of the city fall inside historic and design overlay districts, including the downtown historic district and the Fairpark redevelopment district. Each has its own design standards, so anyone planning exterior changes near downtown should ask Planning first.

Lee County bills the tax, and it is due on or before February 1 for property assessed the preceding year. A single-family, owner-occupied home is Class I and assessed at 10 percent of true value, while other real property is Class II at 15 percent. Real property is revalued at least every four years.

Homestead exemption must be applied for with the Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1. It generally needs a recorded warranty deed, Social Security numbers and the cost of the home. The regular tier is a credit of up to $300, and people 65 or older or totally disabled are exempt on the first $7,500 of assessed value.

The exemption follows the owner. A buyer must own and occupy the house as a primary residence on January 1, with the deed filed with the Chancery Clerk before January 7.

Delinquent property taxes are the other thing to check. The Tax Collector's office posts a last day to pay real property taxes before the August tax sale. After a lien is sold, the owner has two years to pay the taxes plus interest at 1.5 percent per month through the Chancery Clerk. If you owe anything, ask for a payoff figure and have it paid from your sale proceeds so the buyer receives a clear title.

sections.h2: What Mississippi requires and your options
sections.html:
Mississippi Code Section 89-1-503 requires the seller to give the buyer a written property condition disclosure statement as soon as practicable before title transfers. If the buyer receives it after making an offer, the buyer has three days after hand delivery or five days after mailing to cancel in writing.

Tupelo sellers usually choose among three routes: listing with an agent, selling to an investor, or selling directly to a cash buyer who purchases as is. Listing works when a house is in good repair and you can wait. A cash sale is often the more practical route for a house with storm damage, code violations, tax trouble or an estate with several heirs.

Whichever you pick, start with a title search by an attorney or title company, which will show liens and unpaid taxes and whether the seller holds legal title.

Cash Home Buyers speaks with Tupelo sellers about as-is purchases and explains the terms in writing before you decide, so you can compare them against listing.

faqs.q: Do I need a recorded deed to pull a permit in Tupelo?
faqs.a: Yes. The city approves no permits without a current recorded deed, and every application needs a completed form and the deed.

faqs.q: When are Lee County property taxes due?
faqs.a: On or before February 1 for property assessed the preceding year. Payment is accepted the following Monday if February 1 falls on a weekend.

faqs.q: Who do I call about taxes in Lee County?
faqs.a: The Tax Collector is at 662-432-2200 and the Tax Assessor at 662-432-2700. The Homestead Office is at 662-432-2706.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Tupelo house that has code violations?
faqs.a: You can, but a violation letter or citation has to be resolved with Code Enforcement, and unresolved issues can surface in a buyer's inspection. A cash buyer purchasing as is will price the problem in.

faqs.q: How long do I have to redeem a house sold at a tax sale in Lee County?
faqs.a: The owner has two years from the purchase date to pay the taxes plus interest of 1.5 percent per month through the Chancery Clerk.
